  "analysis": "The training data reveals that German legal texts consistently use specific titles (Dr., Mag., Univ.-Prof., etc.) and honorifics (Herr, Frau) to identify persons, often followed by full names and sometimes academic degrees.   "strategy": "Create a set of regex rules that target specific German legal titles and honorifics followed by capitalized name patterns, using context anchors to ensure precision.",

      "name": "Judge_Richter",
      "description": "Matches judges identified by 'Richter' or 'Richterin' followed by optional titles and names.",

      "pattern": "(?:durch\\s+(?:den\\s+|die\\s+)?(?:Richter|Richterin)(?:\\s+(?:Dr\\.|Mag\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.|Univ\\.-Prof\\.in|Hon\\.-Prof\\.|Priv\\.-Doz\\.in|Mag\\.Dr\\.))?\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:,\\s*[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 10,
      "reasoning": "Captures judges in the standard 'Das Bundesfinanzgericht hat durch den Richter [Name]' structure."
    },
    {
      "name": "Representative_Vertreten",
      "description": "Matches persons representing a party, identified by 'vertreten durch' followed by names.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:vertreten\\s+durch\\s+(?:den\\s+|die\\s+)?(?:Dr\\.|Mag\\.|RA\\s+Mag\\.|KommR\\.|StB\\.|Ing\\.?)?\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:,\\s*[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 9,
      "reasoning": "Captures lawyers and representatives in the 'vertreten durch [Name]' structure."
    },
    {
      "name": "Party_Beschwerdesache",
      "description": "Matches the main party (Beschwerdeführer/in) in the 'in der Beschwerdesache [Name]' structure.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:in\\s+der\\s+Beschwerdesache(?:\\s+der)?\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*(?:,\\s*[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 8,
      "reasoning": "Captures the primary party name immediately following the case introduction."
    },
    {
      "name": "Honorific_Herr_Frau",
      "description": "Matches persons preceded by 'Herr' or 'Frau' (including variations like Frau Mag.).",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Herr|Frau)\\s+(?:Mag\\.|Dr\\.|Priv\\.-Doz\\.in)?\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 7,
      "reasoning": "Captures individuals addressed with honorifics in narrative sections or specific mentions."
    },
    {
      "name": "Academic_Title_Person",
      "description": "Matches persons with academic titles like 'Univ.-Prof.', 'Priv.-Doz.in', 'MedR' not covered by judge/representative rules.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Univ\\.-Prof(?:\\.in)?|Priv\\.-Doz\\.in|MedR|Bakk\\. iur\\.|Bakk\\. phil\\.|LLM)\\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)",
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$1",
        "start": "$start",
        "end": "$end",
        "type": "person"
      },
      "output_key": "entities",
      "priority": 6,
      "reasoning": "Captures individuals with specific academic or professional titles that appear as standalone identifiers."
    },
    {
      "name": "Anonymous_Person_M_Dot",
      "description": "Matches anonymized persons like 'Herr M.' or 'Dr. X.Y.' found in legal texts.",
      "format": "regex",
      "pattern": "(?:Herr|Dr\\.?)\\s+([A-Z]\\.)?", 
      "output_template": {
        "text": "$0", 
        "start": "$start", 
        "end": "$end", 
        "type": "person" 
      }, 
      "output_key": "entities", 
      "priority": 5, 
      "reasoning": 
"Captures anonymized references like 'Herr M.' or 'Dr. X.Y.' which are common in redacted legal documents." 
    } 
  ], 
  "deleted_rules": [] 
}

- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority

- GENERALIZE, DON'T MEMORIZE: Rules run on unseen text. Match the *structure* of values, not the exact strings you see in training data.
- USE CONTEXT: The same string can mean different things. Match surrounding words/punctuation and use capture groups ($1) to extract just the value.
- ONE RULE, ONE PATTERN: Multiple focused rules beat one giant regex. Each rule should have a clear, testable reason to exist.
- THINK ADVERSARIALLY: Before writing a rule, ask "what else could this match?" If the answer isn't empty, narrow the pattern or add context.


- Regex patterns (for structured extraction)

REGEX SYNTAX REFERENCE:
- \b word boundaries, (?:...) non-capturing groups, (a|b|c) alternation
- [A-Z] [a-z] \d \s character classes, +*?{n,m} quantifiers
- (?=...) lookahead, (?<=...) lookbehind — match context without consuming it
- (?i) case-insensitive flag

CAPTURE GROUPS ($1) vs FULL MATCH ($0):
- Use $0 in output_template when the entire regex match IS the value you want.
- Use $1 when you need surrounding context to disambiguate — put the value in a capture group.
  With "text": "$1", $start/$end auto-adjust to the group position automatically.

GOOD vs BAD PATTERNS (learn from these):

  BAD:  "\d+"                       — matches every number in the text, most will be wrong type
  GOOD: "(\d+)\s*(?:kg|lbs|oz)"    — only numbers followed by weight units; $1 captures the number

  BAD:  "Alice|Bob|Tokyo"            — memorizes training strings, misses all unseen values
  GOOD: "(?:Mr|Mrs|Dr)\.?\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — captures names after titles

  BAD:  "[A-Z][a-z]+"               — matches any capitalized word (way too broad)
  GOOD: "(?:in|from|at|near)\s+([A-Z][a-z]+(?:\s+[A-Z][a-z]+)*)" — locations after prepositions

  BAD:  "\b\w+@\w+\.\w+\b"         — matches email-like strings but also "user@v1.0"
  GOOD: "(?:email|contact)[:\s]+(\S+@\S+\.\w{2,})" — emails after a label; $1 captures address

  BAD:  one giant regex that handles 5 different sub-patterns
  GOOD: 5 separate rules, each handling one clear case with its own priority
